<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic",
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>

<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent video generation models demonstrate remarkable ability to capture complex physical interactions and scene evolution over time. To leverage their spatiotemporal priors, robotics works have adapted video models for policy learning but introduce complexity by requiring multiple stages of post-training and new architectural components for action generation. In this work, we introduce Cosmos Policy, a simple approach for adapting a large pretrained video model (Cosmos-Predict2) into an effective robot policy through a single stage of post-training on the robot demonstration data collected on the target platform, with no architectural modifications. Cosmos Policy learns to directly generate robot actions encoded as latent frames within the video model’s latent diffusion process, harnessing the model’s pretrained priors and core learning algorithm to capture complex action distributions. Additionally, Cosmos Policy generates future state images and values (expected cumulative rewards), which are similarly encoded as latent frames, enabling test-time planning of action trajectories with higher likelihood of success. In our evaluations, Cosmos Policy achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO and RoboCasa simulation benchmarks (98.5% and 67.1% average success rates, respectively) and the highest average score in challenging real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, outperforming strong diffusion policies trained from scratch, video model-based policies, and state-of-the-art vision-language-action models fine-tuned on the same robot demonstrations. Furthermore, given policy rollout data, Cosmos Policy can learn from experience to refine its world model and value function and leverage model-based planning to achieve even higher success rates in challenging tasks. We release code, models, and training data at <a href="https://research.nvidia.com/labs/dir/cosmos-policy/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://research.nvidia.com/labs/dir/cosmos-policy/</a>.</p>

</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">

</tbody>
</table>
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.16163v1/fig/cosmos_policy_figure1.jpeg" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/157;" width="548" height="157" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>We present Cosmos Policy, a state-of-the-art robot policy fine-tuned from the NVIDIA Cosmos-Predict2-2B video foundation model. Cosmos Policy handles multimodal inputs and multi-view camera images and predicts (1) a robot action chunk, (2) future state (represented by robot proprioception and image observations), and (3) value (expected rewards-to-go at the future state). No architectural changes are made to the base video model, and all modalities are jointly modeled through the video diffusion learning objective.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>
<span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>Correspondence to: Moo Jin Kim <a href="mailto:moojink@cs.stanford.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;moojink@cs.stanford.edu&gt;</a>.
</span></span></span>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large pretrained video generation models have shown impressive ability to generate physically plausible and temporally coherent videos <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wan et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kong et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Unlike pretrained vision-language models—which learn semantic concepts from static image-text pairs and have been popularized as robot policy backbones by recent vision-language-action (VLA) model research (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brohan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Intelligence et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>)—pretrained video generation models learn temporal causality,
implicit physics, and motion patterns from millions of videos.
These spatiotemporal priors hold significant value for robotics applications. In this work, we explore how to effectively leverage video models for robotic control and how they can incorporate policy rollout data to refine their world models and enable more effective planning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Prior works have made significant progress on adapting video models for robotic manipulation, leveraging both robot action data and “action-less” Internet video data to train generalizable policies and perform new tasks with small amounts of demonstrations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liao et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Unitree, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. However, these works often require multiple training stages (e.g., video fine-tuning followed by action module training) and introduce new architectural components, such as separate action diffusers or inverse dynamics models. Other works avoid these complexities by training unified video-action models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, but they do not leverage pretrained video models due to their custom design, limiting their ability to capitalize on the spatiotemporal priors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we address these limitations with <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cosmos Policy</span>: an effective robot policy that is adapted from a pretrained video model (Cosmos-Predict2-2B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA et al., 2025</a>)</cite>) through a single stage of post-training on robot demonstrations. Unlike prior works which carefully design separate action modules and algorithms, Cosmos Policy makes no architectural modifications and instead leverages the pretrained model’s core learning mechanism to capture action distributions. Since video models are effective at modeling complex, high-dimensional, multimodal distributions and can generate temporally coherent videos with hundreds of frames, we hypothesize that their learning algorithms are well-suited for representing actions alongside other modalities. Following this reasoning, we directly fine-tune a video model to simultaneously generate robot actions, future state images, and future state values (expected total cumulative rewards), all of which we encode as latent frames within the model’s latent diffusion sequence. With future state and value predictions, Cosmos Policy can use best-of-N sampling to plan by generating candidate actions, imagining their resulting future states, ranking these states by predicted value, and executing the highest-value action. This search process produces trajectories that are more likely to succeed at the task</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our main contribution is the
Cosmos Policy approach
for fine-tuning pretrained video models to incorporate different modalities that enable
visuomotor control and planning. We evaluate our method in two modes: first as a direct policy (without planning) and then with model-based planning using the future state and value predictions. As a direct policy, Cosmos Policy achieves a new state of the art in both the LIBERO and RoboCasa simulation benchmarks (98.5% and 67.1% average success rates, respectively), outperforming diffusion-based policies trained from scratch, video-based policies (e.g., UVA, Video Policy), and even fine-tuned VLAs (e.g., <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math>, OpenVLA-OFT, CogVLA, UniVLA, DP-VLA, GR00T-N1.5).
It also achieves the highest average success rate (93.6%) among state-of-the-art policies in challenging real-world bimanual manipulation tasks. Further, when enhanced with model-based planning,
we observe
a 12.5 percent higher task completion rate on average in two challenging real-world manipulation tasks. In these experiments, we show that Cosmos Policy can incorporate past experiences from policy rollouts to refine its world model and value function and plan more effectively. Lastly, we compare our model-based planning approach to a model-free variant and study their relative advantages.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Video-based robot policies.</span> Recent works have made great strides in leveraging video models for manipulation. Some methods first fine-tune video models on robot data and then train separate action modules to predict robot actions from generated video frames <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liao et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Unitree, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Other works train unified video-action models that jointly predict future frames and actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, but these approaches do not leverage pretrained video models and thus do not benefit from their spatiotemporal priors. In contrast to these works, we propose a single-stage fine-tuning approach that directly adapts pretrained video models to generate actions (as well as other modalities such as robot proprioceptive state and state values) within their native latent diffusion process.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vision-language-action models.</span> State-of-the-art robotic manipulation policies increasingly leverage large pretrained backbones. Vision-language-action (VLA) models such as RT-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brohan et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, OpenVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Intelligence et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, UniVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and CogVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> fine-tune vision-language models on large-scale robotic imitation data, achieving strong performance across diverse manipulation tasks. While these methods exhibit strong generalization to various semantic concepts unseen in robotic interaction data, they leverage pretrained models that have mostly been trained on static image-text pairs rather than videos. In contrast to these VLAs, we leverage a pretrained video model that has learned spatiotemporal dynamics and implicit physics from predicting future frames for Internet-scale datasets. We hypothesize that this different pretrained backbone can serve as a strong foundation for low-level control policies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">World models and value functions.</span> World models have been used in various ways in robotics and reinforcement learning, from classical model-predictive control to modern neural approaches. Influential works such as Dyna <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sutton, 1991</a>)</cite>, MBPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Janner et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, TD-MPC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hansen et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hansen et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and the Dreamer family of works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2023</a>)</cite> demonstrate the benefits of integrating planning with learning, using learned dynamics models to improve decision making in various control tasks. Recent works have explored different paradigms: FLARE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025</a>)</cite> adds learnable future tokens to diffusion transformer sequences to predict compact representations of future state, SAILOR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al., 2025</a>)</cite> uses separate world and reward models with MPPI planning to iteratively search for better actions and refine the base policy, and Latent Policy Steering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> pretrains world models using optical flow as an embodiment-agnostic action representation and subsequently trains a separate value function to steer the policy towards states with higher rewards. In contrast to these prior works that rely on separate modules for the policy, world model, and value function and typically train from models from scratch, we use a single unified architecture that serves simultaneously as the policy, world model, and value function and initialize from a pretrained video model.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Preliminaries</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cosmos video model.</span> The pretrained video model that serves as the initialization for Cosmos Policy is Cosmos-Predict2-2B-Video2World <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, a latent video diffusion model that receives a starting image and textual description as input and predicts subsequent frames to create a short video.
The model operates over continuous tokens encoded by the Wan2.1 spatiotemporal VAE tokenizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wan et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and is trained using the EDM denoising score matching formulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karras et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. The core training objective for the denoiser network <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> at noise level <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is:
<math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(D_{\theta},\sigma)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{n}}\left[\left\|D_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{0}+\mathbf{n};\sigma,\mathbf{c})-\mathbf{x}_{0}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐧</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐧</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(D_{\theta},\sigma)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{n}}\left[\left\|D_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{0}+\mathbf{n};\sigma,\mathbf{c})-\mathbf{x}_{0}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]</annotation></semantics></math>,
where <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is a clean VAE-encoded image sequence, <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the textual description encoded as T5-XXL embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Raffel et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐧</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐈</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I})</annotation></semantics></math> is i.i.d. Gaussian noise used to corrupt <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> is a diffusion transformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles &amp; Xie, 2023</a>)</cite>
that learns to recover the clean sample given the corrupted one. <math id="S3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> conditions on <math id="S3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}</annotation></semantics></math> via cross-attention and on <math id="S3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> via adaptive layer normalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles &amp; Xie, 2023</a>)</cite>.
The Wan2.1 tokenizer compresses a video sequence of size <math id="S3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1+T)\times H\times W\times 3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1+T)\times H\times W\times 3</annotation></semantics></math> into a latent sequence of size <math id="S3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1+T^{\prime})\times H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>T</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1+T^{\prime})\times H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}\times 16</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T^{\prime}=\frac{T}{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>T</mi><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T^{\prime}=\frac{T}{4}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{\prime}=\frac{H}{8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>H</mi><mn>8</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{\prime}=\frac{H}{8}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{\prime}=\frac{W}{8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>W</mi><mn>8</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{\prime}=\frac{W}{8}</annotation></semantics></math>; these resulting latent frames compose <math id="S3.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> above.
The first frame undergoes no temporal compression
to allow for conditioning on a single input image. During training, a conditioning mask is used to ensure that the first latent frame corresponding to the input image remains clean (without noise) while subsequent frames are corrupted with noise.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MDP formulation and imitation learning.</span> We frame robotic manipulation tasks as finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) defined by the tuple <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\langle S,A,T,R,H\rangle" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\langle S,A,T,R,H\rangle</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> is a set of states, <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> is a set of actions, <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T:S\times A\rightarrow\Pi(S)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T:S\times A\rightarrow\Pi(S)</annotation></semantics></math> is the state transition function, <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R:S\times A\rightarrow\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R:S\times A\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> is the reward function, and <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\in\mathbb{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℕ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\in\mathbb{N}</annotation></semantics></math> is the time horizon, with time steps <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in\{1,2,\ldots,H\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in\{1,2,\ldots,H\}</annotation></semantics></math>. We train a policy <math id="S3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi:S\rightarrow\Pi(A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi:S\rightarrow\Pi(A)</annotation></semantics></math> to maximize rewards, using sparse rewards where <math id="S3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(s_{t},a_{t})=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(s_{t},a_{t})=0</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t&lt;H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t&lt;H</annotation></semantics></math> and terminal rewards <math id="S3.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(s_{H},a_{H})\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(s_{H},a_{H})\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>.
We train policies via imitation learning on expert demonstrations containing state-action pairs. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. (2023)</a></cite>, all policies predict action chunks—sequences of actions for multiple timesteps—to improve motion smoothness and success rates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">World models and value functions. </span>A <em id="S3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">world model</em> <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{T}:S\times A\rightarrow\Pi(S)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{T}:S\times A\rightarrow\Pi(S)</annotation></semantics></math> learns to predict the future state given current state and action, approximating the true environment dynamics. The <em id="S3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">value function</em> for a policy <math id="S3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> at state <math id="S3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> represents expected discounted returns from <math id="S3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> under <math id="S3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>. It is defined as <math id="S3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V^{\pi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi}\left[\sum_{k=t}^{H}\gamma^{k-t}R(s_{k},a_{k})\mid s_{t}=s\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi}\left[\gamma^{H-t}R(s_{H},a_{H})\mid s_{t}=s\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo lspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>H</mi></msubsup><mrow><msup><mi>γ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>γ</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V^{\pi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi}\left[\sum_{k=t}^{H}\gamma^{k-t}R(s_{k},a_{k})\mid s_{t}=s\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi}\left[\gamma^{H-t}R(s_{H},a_{H})\mid s_{t}=s\right]</annotation></semantics></math> in the sparse reward setting, where <math id="S3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> is a discount factor that backpropagates the terminal reward through time. We simply use Monte Carlo returns in this work, labeling each transition in a rollout with the observed return <math id="S3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma^{H-t}R(s_{H},a_{H})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>γ</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma^{H-t}R(s_{H},a_{H})</annotation></semantics></math>. Note: To be precise, we acknowledge that the true state is not fully observable, and the world model predicts future <em id="S3.p3.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">observations</em> (robot proprioception and camera images). However, for notational simplicity and readability, we opt to use the term “state” and treat observations as approximations of the state.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.16163v1/fig/cosmos_policy_diffusion_sequence_v2_main_version.001.jpeg" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/219;" width="548" height="219" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The latent diffusion sequence of Cosmos Policy.</span> We illustrate <em id="S3.F2.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">latent frame injection</em>—the primary mechanism for adapting the pretrained Cosmos-Predict2 into a policy that can predict robot actions, future states, and values without architectural changes. First, raw images are tokenized into latent frames (first row). Then, additional modalities are inserted directly into the latent frame sequence of the video diffusion model (second row). The model is then tasked to denoise the noised latent frames conditioned on the clean frames (third row). See Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Latent Frame Injection: Incorporating New Modalities ‣ 4 Cosmos Policy: Adapting Video Model for Control &amp; Planning ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a> for more details. (Note: For simplicity, this figure does not depict certain implementation details; see Figure <a href="#A1.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ A.1 Latent Injection Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> for a more detailed visualization.)
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Cosmos Policy: Adapting Video Model for Control &amp; Planning</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we discuss how to adapt Cosmos-Predict2 into a unified model that predicts actions, future states, and values. We also discuss leveraging policy rollout data to enable effective planning.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Latent Frame Injection: Incorporating New Modalities</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The original Cosmos-Predict2 model takes as input an image and a textual description to generate a short video for a single camera view. It does not support robot proprioception as input, robot actions or state values as output, nor multiple camera views—all of which are desired or required for manipulation policies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Rather than designing new model components or making architectural modifications as done in prior works, we propose to encode additional modalities as new latent frames that are directly injected into the video model’s latent diffusion sequence. Given a <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1+T^{\prime})\times H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>T</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1+T^{\prime})\times H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}\times 16</annotation></semantics></math> sequence of latent frames, which originally correspond to images in a video, we interleave new modalities (robot state, action chunk, and state values) and images from additional camera views by inserting new latent frames between existing image latent frames. For multiple camera viewpoints, the process is simpler: we simply insert the additional camera images at the image sequence level as shown in the top row of Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) (and the model is subsequently fine-tuned to handle these additional viewpoints).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We now discuss an illustrative example of latent injection for incorporating new modalities. For a robotic platform with two static third-person cameras and a wrist-mounted camera, our latent sequence contains 11 latent frames: (1) a blank placeholder,<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">*</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">*</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">*</span>



            This is an implementation detail that is necessary due to the VAE’s <math id="footnote1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1+\frac{T}{4})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>T</mi><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1+\frac{T}{4})</annotation></semantics></math> temporal compression scheme discussed in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Preliminaries ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, which is commonly used in models such as Cosmos-Predict2 and Wan2.1. See Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Latent Injection Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a> for details.</span></span></span> (2) robot proprioception (e.g., end-effector pose or joint angles), (3) wrist camera image, (4) first third-person camera image, (5) second third-person camera image, (6) action chunk, (7) future robot proprioception, (8) future wrist camera image, (9) future first third-person camera image, (10) future second third-person camera image, and (11) future state value. Among these, (2), (6), (7), and (11) represent new modalities while (3), (5), (8), and (10) represent additional camera views (assuming that the first third-person camera is the “primary” camera). To encode the new modalities as latent frames, we fill each <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}\times C^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}\times C^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> latent volume with normalized and duplicated copies of the robot proprioception, action chunk, or value (where normalization simply consists of rescaling to <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-1,+1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,+1]</annotation></semantics></math>). See Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> for an illustration. This ordering of modalities in the sequence represents <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s,a,s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s,a,s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime}))</annotation></semantics></math>, and it allows for autoregressive decoding of actions, future state, and future state value from left to right (see Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Joint Training of Policy, World Model, &amp; Value Function ‣ 4 Cosmos Policy: Adapting Video Model for Control &amp; Planning ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a> for further discussions on this).
Note that <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> only consist of the observations at time <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t+K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t+K</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively, where <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> is the action chunk size. In other words, we do not use input history nor predict future frames across multiple subsequent timesteps. Lastly, latent injection is flexible and can be adapted for any particular robot setup: for example, for a robot with only one third-person camera, one can simply remove the latent frames corresponding to additional camera viewpoints, and this would result in only seven total latent frames.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">See Figure <a href="#A1.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ A.1 Latent Injection Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> for a more detailed version of Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Implementation details for latent injection are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Latent Injection Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Joint Training of Policy, World Model, &amp; Value Function</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Implementing joint training objectives.</span> Now that we have a latent diffusion scheme that incorporates additional modalities and camera views that are compatible with robotic policy learning, we can adapt the video model into a policy by training on robot data. For each training step, we sample a batch of <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s,a,s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s,a,s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime}))</annotation></semantics></math>
tuples.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">†</span>



            We technically sample the empirical return <math id="footnote2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{t}=\gamma^{H-t}R(s_{H},a_{H})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>γ</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{t}=\gamma^{H-t}R(s_{H},a_{H})</annotation></semantics></math> but write “<math id="footnote2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(s^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(s^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math>” for notational simplicity and readability.</span></span></span> 50 percent of the batch is sampled from the <em id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">demonstrations dataset</em> and is used to train the policy (<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(a,s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(a,s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s)</annotation></semantics></math>), while the other 50 percent is sampled from the <em id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">rollouts dataset</em> and is split into two halves: one half for training the world model (<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p(s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>) and the other half for training the value function (<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(V(s^{\prime})|s,a,s^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(V(s^{\prime})|s,a,s^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math>). The conditioning scheme—i.e., which part of the latent diffusion sequence is used as conditioning and which part is used as the target to generate—determines which of these three functions is being trained (see Figure <a href="#A1.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ A.4.1 Additional Ablation Experiments ‣ A.4 Additional Experiments and Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> for more details). Initially, the rollouts dataset is simply a superset of the demonstrations dataset that also includes failed demonstrations, if they exist. (Failed demonstrations are those that do not successfully complete the task when replayed in the environment due to human error during data collection, e.g., in the LIBERO and RoboCasa simulations where roughly 10 to 20 percent of demonstrations fail when replayed. In certain environments where teleoperation data is collected more carefully, such as our real-world ALOHA environment, failed demonstrations do not exist; in this case, the demonstrations dataset and rollouts dataset are equal.)</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Note that policy and world model training involves auxiliary targets, i.e., the policy is trained to model not just <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(a|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(a|s)</annotation></semantics></math> but rather <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(a,s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(a,s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s)</annotation></semantics></math>, and the world model learns not just <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(s^{\prime}|s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(s^{\prime}|s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> but rather <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p(s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>. We find in Section <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Comparing against State-of-the-Art Imitation Policies without Planning ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a> that the auxiliary supervision improves policy performance. Also, note that the <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(s^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(s^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> predictions are conditioned on the full latent prefix (i.e., all of <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s,a,s^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s,a,s^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math>) during initial Cosmos Policy training. However, when we later fine-tune this base checkpoint on policy rollout data to produce a model with more accurate future state and value predictions, we can choose to condition the value generation on a subset of <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s,a,s^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s,a,s^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> via input masking. The choice of the input mask determines whether the value function represents the state value <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(s^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(s^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> or state-action value <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>; we compare these variations in planning experiments (Section <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Evaluations of Cosmos Policy with Model-Based Planning ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Parallel vs. autoregressive decoding.</span> Since Cosmos Policy learns to both jointly and conditionally predict the targets <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(a,s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a,s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime}))</annotation></semantics></math> based on apportioned training samples, it can generate actions, future states, and values either jointly in parallel or autoregressively from left to right. Parallel decoding offers greater speed, while autoregressive decoding may provide higher-quality predictions and allow for separate checkpoints to be used for the policy versus the world model and value function. For direct policy evaluation without planning, only the actions are required for task execution, while the latter two outputs can be discarded. Therefore, we use parallel decoding in this case. For evaluations with planning, we enable autoregressive decoding for higher-quality future state and value predictions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Planning with Cosmos Policy’s World Model and Value Function</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Cosmos Policy can be deployed as (1) a direct policy without planning or (2) a planning policy using future state and value predictions to search for higher-quality actions. However, training on demonstrations alone is insufficient for effective planning since the data only covers successful outcomes,<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">‡</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">‡</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">‡</span>



            Some demonstration datasets, including the LIBERO simulation benchmark training set, includes suboptimal behaviors that may not lead to success when replayed in the training environment, due to human errors during teleoperation. Typically, however, most (if not all) trajectories in a demonstration dataset used for imitation learning are successful.</span></span></span> which means that the world model and value function see a narrow state-action distribution and may struggle to generalize beyond that distribution. We thus find it critical to collect policy rollout data and learn from these experiences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Learning from rollout experiences.</span> We collect rollout data by deploying Cosmos Policy in diverse initial conditions and recording the trajectory as well as the episode outcome (success/fail or a fractional score). Given the rollout dataset, we fine-tune our Cosmos Policy checkpoint, with heavier weighting on the world model and value function predictions: 90 percent of each training batch is split evenly between training the world model and value function, while only 10 percent is used to train the policy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Once we have the fine-tuned checkpoint for refined world modeling and policy learning, we propose <em id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">dual deployment</em>: the original Cosmos Policy checkpoint serves as the policy (we thus call it the “policy model”), while the refined checkpoint serves as the world model and value function (we thus call it the “planning model”). This ensures that the refined world model and value function are trained on on-policy data collected by the original policy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model-based planning.</span> Given the policy model and the planning model, we implement best-of-N sampling as follows: (1) sample multiple action proposals from the policy, (2) use the planning model to predict the future state and value for each proposal, (3) select and deploy the action that leads to the predicted state with the highest predicted value.
For greater accuracy and better modeling of potentially multimodal future state and value distributions, we ensemble the predictions by querying the world model three times per action and the value function five times per future state, resulting in fifteen total value predictions for each action proposal. We aggregate these via “majority mean”: we determine whether the majority predict success or failure (via a fixed threshold) and then average values within the majority group. This approach is more robust to outliers than naive averaging when value predictions are bimodal or exhibit high variance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To speed up the search process, we use parallelized inference, using N GPUs in best-of-N sampling. We also execute the full action chunk (rather only part of it, as done in receding-horizon control) to avoid further increases in computational cost.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.16163v1/fig/cosmos_policy_aloha_rollouts.001.jpeg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/157;" width="548" height="157" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cosmos Policy in the ALOHA robot tasks.</span> Cosmos Policy can successfully execute real-world robotic control tasks that require long-horizon, high-precision manipulation and have high action multimodality.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate Cosmos Policy to answer four key questions: <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Q1)</span> How does Cosmos Policy compare with state-of-the-art imitation learning policies when used as a direct policy? <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Q2)</span> How important are different components of Cosmos Policy? <span id="S5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Q3)</span> Can Cosmos Policy leverage rollout experiences and learn an accurate world model and value function for effective planning? <span id="S5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Q4)</span> Is it more effective to search using a world model and state value function or a Q-value function (a model-free variation)? We answer these through simulated and real-world evaluations spanning single-arm and dual-arm manipulation tasks.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now describe the three task suites used in our evaluations. Note that further training and evaluation details are available in Appendices <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Training Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a> and <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 Evaluation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LIBERO simulation benchmark.</span> The LIBERO benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> consists of a variety of environments and tasks featuring a single Franka Emika Panda robot arm. The four primary task suites include LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, LIBERO-Goal, and LIBERO-Long (also called LIBERO-10); these assess a policy’s ability to handle different spatial layouts, objects, language-specified goals, and long-horizon tasks, respectively. Each task suite provides a training dataset of 500 total demonstrations (10 tasks and 50 demonstrations each). Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2024)</a></cite>, we filter unsuccessful demonstrations for policy training but use the full unfiltered set for world model and value function training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RoboCasa simulation benchmark.</span> The RoboCasa benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nasiriany et al., 2024</a>)</cite> consists of 24 static kitchen manipulation tasks featuring a single Franka Emika Panda robot arm. We follow the evaluation protocol of several prior works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nasiriany et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Specifically, for each task, success rate is evaluated over 50 trials across five evaluation scenes with different floor plans and styles (10 trials per scene), and the average success rate is computed across all 24 tasks over 3 random seeds (3600 trials total). Unlike LIBERO evaluations, the RoboCasa evaluations only consist of <em id="S5.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">unseen object instances</em>, and two of the five scenes per task include styles <em id="S5.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">never encountered in the training data</em>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The benchmark provides a set of 50 human-teleoperated demonstrations for each task and an additional set of 1000 demonstrations generated via MimicGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mandlekar et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and prior works have shown clear increases in success rates from using larger training datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nasiriany et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. However, to assess the relative data efficiency of Cosmos Policy compared to prior works, we train our method on the 50 human-teleoperated demonstrations alone. Similar to LIBERO data preprocessing, we filter unsuccessful demonstrations for policy training but use the full unfiltered dataset for world model and value function training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Real-world ALOHA robot tasks.</span> The ALOHA platform <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2023</a>)</cite> consists of two ViperX 300 S robot arms with three cameras: one top-down and two wrist-mounted. We reduce the controller frequency from 50 Hz to 25 Hz for computational efficiency. All policies take as input robot proprioceptive state (14 joint angles), three camera images, and task descriptions, predicting action chunks of 50 timesteps (2 seconds).<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">§</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">§</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">§</span>



            Diffusion Policy is an exception, as it predicts 48-timestep action chunks since the implementation requires a multiple of 4.</span></span></span> We deploy the full action chunk before requerying the policy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our evaluation suite consists of four challenging bimanual manipulation tasks (shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 Planning with Cosmos Policy’s World Model and Value Function ‣ 4 Cosmos Policy: Adapting Video Model for Control &amp; Planning ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>): (1) “put X on plate” (80 demos): place objects on a plate based on language instructions, testing language following; (2) “fold shirt” (15 demos): fold one of three T-shirts in multiple steps, testing long-horizon contact-rich manipulation; (3) “put candies in bowl” (45 demos): collect scattered candies, testing ability to handle multimodal grasp sequences; and (4) “put candy in ziploc bag” (45 demos): open and place items in a ziploc slider bag, testing high-precision manipulation with millimeter tolerance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The evaluations consist of both in-distribution and out-of-distribution testing conditions, with 101 trials total per method across all tasks. We ensure fair comparison between methods by using the same fixed set of initial states for each method.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S5.T2.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:196.8pt;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Table 1: </span><span id="S5.T2.fig1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LIBERO simulation benchmark results.</span> Success rates (SR) across four LIBERO benchmark task suites <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Cosmos Policy success rates are averaged over 500 trials for each suite (10 tasks × 50 episodes) and three random seeds (6000 trials total). Our method achieves highest performance overall, even outperforming fine-tuned state-of-the-art vision-language-action (VLA) models.
</figcaption>

<tr id="S5.T2.fig1.3.1.12" class="ltx_tr" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF99;">

<td id="S5.T2.fig1.3.1.12.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r"><span id="S5.T2.fig1.3.1.12.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF99;">100.0</span></td>

</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S5.T2.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:194.8pt;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Table 2: </span><span id="S5.T2.fig2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RoboCasa simulation benchmark results.</span> Success rates (SR) across 24 kitchen manipulation tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nasiriany et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Cosmos Policy success rates are averaged over 50 trials for each task and three random seeds (3600 trials total).
