</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Comparing against State-of-the-Art Imitation Policies without Planning</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here we aim to answer questions <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q1</span> and <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q2</span> posed in the beginning of this section. We answer <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q1</span> by comparing Cosmos Policy as a direct policy (without planning) with state-of-the-art imitation learning policies and assessing their relative effectiveness. We answer <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q2</span> by ablating various components of Cosmos Policy and analyzing the resulting effects on task performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Methods in comparison.</span> In LIBERO and Robocasa, we compare against recent top-performing methods including diffusion-based policies trained from scratch (Diffusion Policy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, Dita <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>), video model-based policies (UVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, UWM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Video Policy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>), and fine-tuned VLA models (<math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math>, OpenVLA-OFT, CogVLA, UniVLA, DP-VLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, GR00T-N1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al., 2025</a>)</cite>). In real-world ALOHA evaluations, we compare against a competitive subset of policies that have demonstrated strong performance in real-world bimanual manipulation tasks: Diffusion Policy, OpenVLA-OFT+, <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results.</span> Tables <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> show the performance of Cosmos Policy and prior works in LIBERO and RoboCasa, respectively, while Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Comparing against State-of-the-Art Imitation Policies without Planning ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows performance on the ALOHA robot. We find that Cosmos Policy achieves highest overall performance in all three domains, while establishing a new state of the art in the LIBERO and RoboCasa benchmarks with 98.5% and 67.1% average success rates, respectively. These results demonstrate Cosmos Policy’s strong multi-task manipulation performance in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization scenarios. In addition, in ALOHA robot evaluations, we find that Cosmos Policy outperforms fine-tuned VLAs <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math> and OpenVLA-OFT+—which have been pretrained on large amounts of robotic imitation data—despite not having benefited from similar large-scale action supervision. This finding suggests that video model priors provide a strong initialization for control policies without requiring additional action-labeled robot data. Sample Cosmos Policy rollouts are visualized in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 Planning with Cosmos Policy’s World Model and Value Function ‣ 4 Cosmos Policy: Adapting Video Model for Control &amp; Planning ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.16163v1/fig/aloha_task_performance_results_v2.001.jpeg" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:521/141;" width="521" height="141" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span><span id="S5.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Real-world ALOHA robot evaluation results.</span> We evaluate state-of-the-art policies on a suite of four tasks and measure the score, which represents average percent completion of each task. Cosmos Policy achieves highest overall score, outperforming all other methods in three of four tasks.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.16163v1/fig/pi05_openvlaoft_aloha_rollouts.001.jpeg" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/150;" width="548" height="150" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span><span id="S5.F5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Common failure modes of <math id="S5.F5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math> and OpenVLA-OFT+ on two challenging ALOHA robot tasks.</span> <span id="S5.F5.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Left:</span> <math id="S5.F5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math> struggles to execute a high-precision grasp and loses grip of the ziploc bag. <span id="S5.F5.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Right:</span> OpenVLA-OFT+ reaches between two candies rather than towards one, suggesting difficulty with modeling the highly multimodal action distribution.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.16163v1/fig/cosmos_policy_planning_rollouts.001.jpeg" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:439/176;" width="439" height="176" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span><span id="S5.F6.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">World model predictions: base Cosmos Policy vs. fine-tuned checkpoint.</span> <span id="S5.F6.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top:</span> The base Cosmos Policy’s world model may fail to predict errors such as losing grasp of the ziploc bag slider, as it is only trained on demonstrations. <span id="S5.F6.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bottom:</span> After fine-tuning on policy rollout data, the world model more accurately predicts the resulting state, enabling more effective planning and eventual episode success.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Qualitatively, we find that while the fine-tuned VLAs show strong performance on the first two tasks, they encounter difficulties in the last two tasks—“put candies in bowl” and “put candy in ziploc bag”—which require handling high action multimodality and executing high-precision grasps, respectively. Figure <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 Comparing against State-of-the-Art Imitation Policies without Planning ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> visualizes two common failure modes of <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math> and OpenVLA-OFT+: (1) <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math>, despite showing highly competitive performance on the first three tasks, struggles to reliably handle the ziploc bag, often missing the initial grasp of the slider with the right arm or not grasping the left side of the bag securely enough with the left arm. (2) OpenVLA-OFT+ often reaches in between two candies rather than directly going for one; we hypothesize that its L1 regression of actions leads to inaccurate modeling of the action distribution in tasks with high multimodality. Compared to these methods, Cosmos Policy handles both high multimodality and high precision with substantially greater reliability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ablation experiments.</span> Recall from Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Joint Training of Policy, World Model, &amp; Value Function ‣ 4 Cosmos Policy: Adapting Video Model for Control &amp; Planning ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a> that Cosmos Policy’s policy and world model training involves additional targets which provide additional supervision: the policy learns to jointly predict <math id="S5.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(a,s^{\prime},v(s^{\prime}))|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(a,s^{\prime},v(s^{\prime}))|s)</annotation></semantics></math> instead of <math id="S5.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(a|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(a|s)</annotation></semantics></math>, and the world model learns to jointly predict <math id="S5.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p(s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> instead of <math id="S5.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(s^{\prime}|s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(s^{\prime}|s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>. To evaluate the effect of these auxiliary learning objectives, we train a version of Cosmos Policy without them by masking the loss on the additional targets. In addition, we assess the importance of the video model priors by training Cosmos Policy from randomly initialized weights. We use the same number of gradient steps as the full policy for both of these variants. As shown in Table <a href="#A1.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ A.4.1 Additional Ablation Experiments ‣ A.4 Additional Experiments and Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, removing the auxiliary losses leads to a 1.5% absolute drop in average success rate while training from scratch leads to a 3.9% drop, suggesting that these components are important for maximal performance. We further evaluate Cosmos Policy trained from scratch on the ALOHA robot for additional supporting evidence and find that it obtains an average score of 80.8 on the “fold shirt” task, which is 18.7 points lower than the full Cosmos Policy. Qualitatively, the from-scratch variant exhibits jerky motions that may damage the robot over prolonged deployment, so we halt further evaluations with it. Additional ablation studies on the Cosmos Policy design and joint training scheme are discussed in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS4.SSS1" title="A.4.1 Additional Ablation Experiments ‣ A.4 Additional Experiments and Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.4.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Evaluations of Cosmos Policy with Model-Based Planning</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here we aim to answer <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q3</span> by evaluating Cosmos Policy when deployed with model-based planning (as described in Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Planning with Cosmos Policy’s World Model and Value Function ‣ 4 Cosmos Policy: Adapting Video Model for Control &amp; Planning ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>), and <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q4</span> by analyzing how the proposed model-based approach compares different variants of planning, such as directly learning a Q-value function without a world model. Since our base Cosmos Policy already obtains high success rates in LIBERO and on the first two ALOHA robot tasks, we focus our study on the last two more challenging ALOHA robot tasks (“put candies in bowl” and “put candy in ziploc bag”), where there is more room for improvement. Further, we focus on a more challenging set of initial conditions (difficult in-distribution conditions and OOD conditions) and assess whether planning can enhance performance in these settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Rollout data collection.</span> To refine Cosmos Policy’s world model and value function predictions and enable more effective planning, we gather a rollout dataset that we use for post-training.
Conveniently, by running the prior direct policy evaluations, we have already aggregated 505 policy rollouts across all policies. Adding to this, we collect 143 more rollouts from Cosmos Policy for the ”put candy in ziploc bag” task. The additional episodes are important for this task since training an accurate world model for it is particularly challenging due to low camera observability from the robot’s self-occlusion and highly stochastic environment dynamics where even millimeter differences in control can dictate success or failure. We fine-tune the base Cosmos Policy checkpoint on this pool of 648 rollouts to produce a refined “planning model” for world modeling and value prediction, as described in Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Planning with Cosmos Policy’s World Model and Value Function ‣ 4 Cosmos Policy: Adapting Video Model for Control &amp; Planning ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparing different value function formulations.</span> When fine-tuning the base Cosmos Policy checkpoint on the rollout dataset, we use three independent formulations for value function training by using input masks to condition the value predictions on different subsets of inputs: <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(s^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(s^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> (mask out <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>) or <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> (mask out <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>). The <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(s^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(s^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> variant requires a world model to predict the future state before the value can be estimated, while the <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> variant enables model-free planning by directly predicting Q-values without future state predictions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results.</span> We observe that model-based planning using the <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(s^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(s^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> formulation consistently improves success rates over the base Cosmos Policy without planning, as shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 5.3 Evaluations of Cosmos Policy with Model-Based Planning ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. In ALOHA tasks, we observe a 12.5-point average score increase in the two challenging manipulation tasks which involve multimodal grasp sequences and high-precision manipulation. This is a notable improvement given the limited amount of rollout data available for refining the planning model. Qualitatively, we find that the fine-tuned planning model predicts future states more accurately (see Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5.2 Comparing against State-of-the-Art Imitation Policies without Planning ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>) and can plan more effectively, ultimately avoiding making mistakes that the base Cosmos Policy makes, such as losing grasp of the slider while opening the ziploc bag. When comparing model-based (<math id="S5.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(s^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(s^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math>) versus model-free (<math id="S5.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>) planning variants, we observe higher performance with the former, which we attribute its ability to leverage learned environment dynamics for more effective and sample-efficient planning. Given a limited amount of rollout data, we expect difficulty with learning an accurate Q-function and suspect that the model may also overfit given higher input dimensionality.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.16163v1/fig/planning_results.001.jpeg" id="S5.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:439/167;" width="439" height="167" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span><span id="S5.F7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model-based planning results.</span> We evaluate the base Cosmos Policy on challenging initial states for the last two ALOHA robot tasks, and compare it with two planning variants (model-based and model-free). We find that the model-based variant (<math id="S5.F7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(s^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(s^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math>) leads to highest overall performance.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Discussion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We presented Cosmos Policy, a state-of-the-art robot policy fine-tuned from the Cosmos-Predict2 video foundation model that demonstrates strong performance in LIBERO, RoboCasa, and ALOHA robot environments. We also show that incorporating policy rollout data to refine world model and value function predictions enables effective model-based planning. <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Limitations and future work:</span> We observe substantially lower inference speed when using model-based planning (e.g., around 5 seconds to produce one action chunk), which may limit applicability to dynamic tasks. How to speed up the search is an important direction for future study. In addition, effective planning requires substantial rollout data to achieve accurate predictions beyond the demonstration distribution. Learning from fewer rollouts would increase the accessibility of our approach. Lastly, we focus on best-of-N planning with one layer in the search tree; extending the world model’s prediction horizon and planning to greater depths could potentially lead to more effective search.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Reproducibility Statement</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We release model checkpoints, training data, and code (including training and evaluation scripts) on our project website. Further training and evaluation details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Training Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a> and <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 Evaluation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>, respectively.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Appendix</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Latent Injection Implementation
Details</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As discussed in Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Latent Frame Injection: Incorporating New Modalities ‣ 4 Cosmos Policy: Adapting Video Model for Control &amp; Planning ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>, Cosmos Policy learns to condition on and generate new non-image modalities (such as actions, robot proprioception, and values) through a mechanism called <em id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">latent injection</em>. Figure <a href="#A1.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ A.1 Latent Injection Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> provides a detailed visualization of how latent injection operates within Cosmos Policy’s latent diffusion sequence.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The process begins with a sequence of images from multiple camera viewpoints, along with blank (all-zero) images that serve as placeholders for the new modalities to be injected. Once the video model’s VAE tokenizer converts this image sequence into latent frames, we perform latent injection by overwriting the latent frames corresponding to the blank placeholder images with normalized and duplicated copies of the robot proprioception, action chunk, and value. Normalization rescales each modality to the range <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-1,+1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,+1]</annotation></semantics></math>, while duplication resolves the shape mismatch between the low-dimensional vectors and the target latent volumes.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For instance, consider an action chunk with shape <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\times d_{act}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\times d_{act}</annotation></semantics></math>. We first normalize each action dimension to <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-1,+1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,+1]</annotation></semantics></math>, and then flatten the array into a <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(K\times d_{act})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(K\times d_{act})</annotation></semantics></math> vector. This vector is duplicated <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{(H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}\times C^{\prime})}{(K\times d_{act})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{(H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}\times C^{\prime})}{(K\times d_{act})}</annotation></semantics></math> times (where <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(H^{\prime},W^{\prime},C^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(H^{\prime},W^{\prime},C^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> represents the shape of a single latent frame), reshaped into a <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}\times C^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}\times C^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> volume, and used to overwrite the corresponding target latent frame. We apply an analogous process for robot proprioception and value, though their initial shapes differ.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Following latent injection, we corrupt portions of the latent sequence by adding randomly sampled Gaussian noise scaled by a randomly sampled noise level (see Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2.SSS1" title="A.2.1 Cosmos Policy Noise Distribution ‣ A.2 Training Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2.1</span></a> for details). Cosmos Policy is then trained to denoise these corrupted portions of the latent diffusion sequence while conditioning on the clean (uncorrupted) portions. Although latent injection introduces new modalities that were not present during the base video model’s pretraining, we find that the model can still learn to generate them effectively through fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">At inference time, Cosmos Policy generates clean (denoised) latent frames. Extracting the new modalities involves reversing the latent injection process described above. For example, to extract the action chunk prediction from the generated action latent, we compute the average action chunk across all <math id="A1.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{(H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}\times C^{\prime})}{(K\times d_{act})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{(H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}\times C^{\prime})}{(K\times d_{act})}</annotation></semantics></math> copies in the latent volume. We then un-normalize the action chunk back to its original scale and deploy either the full action chunk or a portion of it on the robot. On the other hand, extracting the value is much simpler since it is a scalar (represented by a single floating point number): we simply take the average across the full latent volume and then un-normalize to the original range (<math id="A1.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,+1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,+1]</annotation></semantics></math>). Note that extracting non-image modalities like these does not require any VAE decoding since these elements were directly injected into the latent space during training.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F8" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.16163v1/fig/cosmos_policy_diffusion_sequence_v2_detailed_for_appendix.001.jpeg" id="A1.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/202;" width="548" height="202" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span><span id="A1.F8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Detailed view of the latent diffusion sequence of Cosmos Policy.</span> This is a more detailed version of Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> which shows implementation details. As illustrated in the top row, blank (all zero) images are inserted into the input image sequence, and these images are encoded into latent frames by the VAE tokenizer. Then, in the middle row, these placeholder latent frames are completely overwritten by latent injection of new modalities (robot proprioception, actions, and value). Note that a placeholder image is set apart at the beginning of the sequence due to the video model’s tokenization scheme, which encodes the first image by itself while the rest of the images are temporally compressed in groups of four (as discussed in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Preliminaries ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). Therefore, to ensure that current timestep observations and future timestep observations have similarly structured latent representations, we place them after the blank first latent frame in the video diffusion sequence. In addition, since we wish to have one latent frame for each modality and camera viewpoint, we construct four identical copies of each image, as shown in the top row. Each group of four identical images corresponds to a single timestep rather than four timesteps).
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Training Details</h3>

<section id="A1.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.2.1 </span>Cosmos Policy Noise Distribution</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Changes to noise levels during training and inference.</span> We find that the base Cosmos-Predict2 model’s <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> (noise level) sampling scheme is suitable for video generation tasks but not the most effective for robot policy training. The latter requires generations to be very precise since the generated actions are used to directly control a robot and small imprecisions can lead to catastrophic failures. Therefore, to improve the accuracy of the generations at test time, we modify the noise level sampling scheme at both train and test time.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The base model’s original noise distribution is a log-normal distribution, similar to the EDM formulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karras et al., 2022</a>)</cite>: <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{ln}(\sigma)\sim\mathcal{N}(P_{\text{mean}},P_{\text{std}}^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>ln</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>mean</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mtext>std</mtext><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{ln}(\sigma)\sim\mathcal{N}(P_{\text{mean}},P_{\text{std}}^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{mean}}=1.39,P_{\text{std}}=1.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>mean</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1.39</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>std</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1.2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{mean}}=1.39,P_{\text{std}}=1.2</annotation></semantics></math> for Cosmos-Predict2-2B (see Figure <a href="#A1.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ A.2.1 Cosmos Policy Noise Distribution ‣ A.2 Training Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, left). For action generation, we observe that the low weight on higher noise levels causes inaccurate action predictions during sampling. Diffusion generation begins with pure noise scaled by <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\text{max}}=80" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>80</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\text{max}}=80</annotation></semantics></math> and iteratively denoises over multiple steps as <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> decreases to <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\text{min}}\approx 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>min</mtext></msub><mo>≈</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\text{min}}\approx 0</annotation></semantics></math>. At each step, the network predicts the noise at the current <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> level to progressively recover a clean sample. Since the log-normal distribution concentrates training weight at lower noise levels, the model has insufficient signal at the high-<math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> regime where generation begins, causing poor initial denoising and cascading errors. While this may not be critical for image and video generation, we find it is harmful for action generation, where predictions must be precise.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, for Cosmos Policy training, we use a hybrid log-normal-uniform distribution with greater weight on larger noise levels (see Figure <a href="#A1.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ A.2.1 Cosmos Policy Noise Distribution ‣ A.2 Training Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, right). To implement this, we sample from the original log-normal distribution with probability 0.7 and from a uniform distribution over <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1.0,85.0]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1.0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>85.0</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1.0,85.0]</annotation></semantics></math> with probability 0.3, creating a log-normal distribution with an extended tail at higher <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> values. We find this empirically improves action prediction accuracy and overall success rate. We chose the 0.7/0.3 split to stay close to the original distribution while extending the high-<math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> tail; these probability values were not tuned.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">At test time, we find that the final denoising steps with <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma\approx 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma\approx 0</annotation></semantics></math> are less accurate than earlier steps at larger <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> values, likely due to the low signal-to-noise ratio at very small noise levels. Therefore, when sampling from Cosmos Policy, we set a higher lower bound with <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\text{min}}=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>min</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\text{min}}=4</annotation></semantics></math> (rather than <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\text{min}}=0.002" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>min</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.002</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\text{min}}=0.002</annotation></semantics></math> as in the original EDM formulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karras et al., 2022</a>)</cite>) while keeping <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\text{max}}=80" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>80</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\text{max}}=80</annotation></semantics></math>. This higher lower bound empirically improves prediction accuracy at inference time for actions, future states, and values, as measured by lower L1 loss on training and validation samples.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.16163v1/fig/noise_schedules_figure.001.jpeg" id="A1.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/179;" width="548" height="179" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span><span id="A1.F9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Base model noise distribution vs. Cosmos Policy’s adjusted noise distribution.</span> We change the base Cosmos-Predict2 video model’s log-normal noise distribution (left) into a hybrid log-normal-uniform distribution (right) with more weight on higher noise levels. This modification empirically leads to more accurate generations at test time. See a detailed explanation in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2.SSS1" title="A.2.1 Cosmos Policy Noise Distribution ‣ A.2 Training Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2.1</span></a>.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.2.2 </span>LIBERO Training Details</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train Cosmos Policy for 40K gradient steps using 64 H100 GPUs with global batch size 1920 (taking 48 hours total). The base Cosmos-Predict2 model is fully fine-tuned (all model weights). We train the policy to predict an action chunk size of 16 timesteps and execute the full chunk at test time before requerying. After 40K gradient steps, the policy’s action L1 training loss is 0.012, future proprio L1 training loss is 0.007, future wrist image latent L1 training loss is 0.068, future third-person image latent L1 training loss is 0.036, and value function L1 loss is 0.007. All non-image modalities are normalized to the range <math id="A1.SS2.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-1,+1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,+1]</annotation></semantics></math> for training. (Note that these are single-step training losses given varying <math id="A1.SS2.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> (noise levels) as input, rather than losses on generations from the multi-step diffusion sampling used during policy inference.) The magnitudes of these losses imply that the model more quickly learns to predict actions, proprioception, and values than images.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.2.3 </span>RoboCasa Training Details</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train Cosmos Policy for 45K gradient steps using 32 H100 GPUs with global batch size 800 (taking 48 hours total). The base Cosmos-Predict2 model is fully fine-tuned (all model weights). We train the policy to predict an action chunk of 32 timesteps and execute 16 steps before requerying. After 45K gradient steps, the policy’s action L1 training loss is 0.016, future proprio L1 training loss is 0.007, future wrist image latent L1 training loss is 0.084, future third-person images latents L1 training loss is 0.048, and value function L1 loss is 0.007. All non-image modalities are normalized to the range <math id="A1.SS2.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-1,+1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,+1]</annotation></semantics></math> for training.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.2.4 </span>ALOHA Training Details</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For Cosmos Policy and all other methods in our ALOHA robot evaluations, we train a single policy on all four tasks combined (185 total demonstrations). Cosmos Policy is trained for 50K gradient steps using 8 H100 GPUs with a global batch size of 200, taking 48 hours total. The base Cosmos-Predict2 model is fully fine-tuned (all model weights). We train with an action chunk size of 50 timesteps (spanning 2 seconds given a 25 Hz controller) and execute the full chunk before requerying. After 50K gradient steps, the policy’s action L1 training loss is 0.010, future proprio L1 training loss is 0.008, future wrist images latents L1 training loss is 0.097, future third-person image latent L1 training loss is 0.085, and value function L1 loss is 0.007. All non-image modalities are normalized to the range <math id="A1.SS2.SSS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-1,+1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,+1]</annotation></semantics></math> for training.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For fair comparison with Cosmos Policy, we fine-tune <math id="A1.SS2.SSS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.SS2.SSS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, and OpenVLA-OFT+ using the same computational budget: 48 hours on 8 H100 GPUs. Despite identical wall-clock time for fine-tuning, differences in training iteration speed across models and training frameworks result in substantial variation in the number of gradient steps completed: <math id="A1.SS2.SSS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS2.SSS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> are fine-tuned for 400K gradient steps (batch size 256), while OpenVLA-OFT+ is fine-tuned for 32K gradient steps (batch size 96 given gradient accumulation 4). We train for this seemingly large number of gradient steps across all methods because we observe that training loss continues to decrease and task execution quality generally improves with extended training. Finally, for the significantly smaller Diffusion Policy, which only contains approximately 150M parameters (as opposed to 2-7B for the other methods), we train from scratch on 1 H100 GPU for 48 hours, resulting in 190 epochs, equivalent to 72K gradient steps (batch size 350). Like Cosmos Policy, all policies are trained to predict an action chunk of 50 timesteps (except Diffusion Policy, which predicts 48 steps since it requires a multiple of 4), and the full chunk is executed before the model is requeried at test time.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Evaluation Details</h3>

<section id="A1.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.3.1 </span>General Cosmos Policy Evaluation Details</h4>

<div id="A1.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Number of denoising steps and parallel vs. autoregressive generation.</span> When evaluating Cosmos Policy as a direct policy, we predict actions, future state, and future state value altogether in parallel. Since direct policy evaluations do not use planning, we simply discard the future state and value predictions (though these can be saved for visualizations of the policy’s intent and estimates of task progress). We use 5 denoising steps for LIBERO and RoboCasa and 10 denoising steps for ALOHA. On the other hand, when evaluating Cosmos Policy with model-based planning, we autoregressively generate actions, then future state, and then future state value. In the real-world evaluations with planning, we use 10 denoising steps for the actions, 5 for the future state, and 5 for the value. In addition, we use an ensemble of 3 future state predictions and an ensemble of 5 value predictions to robustify the estimates.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.3.2 </span>Real-World ALOHA Robot Evaluation Details</h4>

<div id="A1.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Number of trials and initial conditions.</span> We evaluate every method in the real ALOHA robot experiments with 101 total trials: 30 trials for “put X on plate”, 20 trials for “fold shirt”, 25 trials for “put candies in bowl”, and 26 trials for “put candy in ziploc bag”. For each task, we test on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization scenarios with respect to the training demonstration dataset (see Figures <a href="#A1.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ A.3.2 Real-World ALOHA Robot Evaluation Details ‣ A.3 Evaluation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> and <a href="#A1.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ A.3.2 Real-World ALOHA Robot Evaluation Details ‣ A.3 Evaluation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> for visualizations). We describe the details of the test conditions below:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="A1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>
<div id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">“put X on plate”: 20 in-distribution + 10 OOD trials. For in-distribution trials, the two objects (purple eggplant and brown chicken wing) are placed in the same row along the horizontal axis of the table, with varying position along the vertical axis. For OOD trials, the objects are not constrained to be in the same row and the positions are more varied. Max time limit is 350 timesteps (14 seconds).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">“fold shirt”: 12 in-distribution + 8 OOD trials. For in-distribution trials, we use three T-shirts of different colors (blue with white stripes, plain white, and brown camouflage) with four fixed initial positions on the table (back, front, left middle, right middle). These three T-shirts were seen at data collection time (five demos for each of the three shirt, for 15 training demos total). For OOD trials, we use an unseen pink T-shirt with the same four initial positions for the first four trials, and the seen blue-with-white-stripes shirt with unseen distractor objects placed on the table (other shirts folded up and placed on the sides or corners of the table, serving as visual distractors). Max time limit is 1600 timesteps (64 seconds).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>
<div id="A1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">“put candies in bowl”: 15 in-distribution + 10 OOD trials. For in-distribution trials, we place 5 candies in front of a large metal bowl, with a roughly even balance of candies on the left versus right half of the table. For OOD trials, we either (a) place 5 candies in front or behind a large metal bowl with uneven amounts of candies on the left versus right half, or (b) place 5 candies in front or behind an unseen smaller orange bowl. Max time limit is 1100 timesteps (44 seconds).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>
<div id="A1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">“put candy in ziploc bag”: 20 in-distribution trials + 6 OOD trials. For in-distribution trials, we place a pink ziploc bag filled half full with candies in the middle of the table with varying initial position along the vertical axis, and one piece of candy to its right (also varying along the vertical axis). For OOD trials, we replace the pink ziploc bag with an unseen blue ziploc bag that is filled to about 75 percent full (more than seen during training), which requires more firm grasps when grasping the bag so that it does not slip out of grasp as the robot manipulates it. Max time limit is 1100 timesteps (44 seconds).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.16163v1/fig/iid_initial_positions.jpeg" id="A1.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:548/449;" width="548" height="449" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span><span id="A1.F10.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">In-distribution initial conditions for ALOHA robot evaluations.</span> Here we show sample initial positions used for evaluating policies in conditions similar to the training demonstrations.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A1.F11" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.16163v1/fig/ood_initial_positions.jpeg" id="A1.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/299;" width="548" height="299" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 11: </span><span id="A1.F11.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Out-of-distribution initial conditions for ALOHA robot evaluations.</span> Here we show sample initial positions used for evaluating policies in unseen test conditions.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS3.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scoring rubrics.</span> Here we describe how each policy rollout is scored between 0 and 100 points. Each score represents what percent of the task has been successfully completed. We use score instead of success rate since a binary metric does not capture fine-grained details.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="A1.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>
<div id="A1.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">“put X on plate”: 50 points for touching the correct target object. 50 points for putting the correct target object on the plate.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>
<div id="A1.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">“fold shirt”: 10 points for each of the following stages: (1) grasped bottom edge of shirt, (2) folded in half, (3) grasped both sleeves, (4) folded sleeves in, (5) grasped bottom edge of shirt, (6) folded in half again, (7) grasped right edge of shirt, (8) folded in half again, (9) released the shirt from grasp, (10) pushed shirt to center of table. In the end, 10 points are deducted if a part of the shirt (e.g. sleeve) sticks out due to an incomplete fold.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>
<div id="A1.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">“put candies in bowl”: 20 points for each of 5 candies grasped and placed into the bowl.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>
<div id="A1.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">“put candy in ziploc bag”: 20 points for each of the following stages: (1) grasped ziploc bag opener with right arm, (2) grasped ziploc bag’s upper-left corner with left arm, (3) opened bag at least halfway by pulling the opener with right arm, (4) grasped candy with right arm, (5) placed candy inside bag.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.SSS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Detailed in-distribution vs. OOD evaluation scores.</span> Table <a href="#A1.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ A.3.2 Real-World ALOHA Robot Evaluation Details ‣ A.3 Evaluation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the breakdown of in-distribution and out-of-distribution scores for every method across the ALOHA robot task suite. Cosmos Policy achieves highest aggregate success rates, though <math id="A1.SS3.SSS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math> shows slightly better performance specifically in OOD test scenarios.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T3" class="ltx_table">

<section id="A1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.4 </span>Additional Experiments and Details</h3>

<section id="A1.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.4.1 </span>Additional Ablation Experiments</h4>

<figure id="A1.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span><span id="A1.T4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cosmos Policy ablations in LIBERO.</span> Here we report the results of two independent ablations: (1) In Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Joint Training of Policy, World Model, &amp; Value Function ‣ 4 Cosmos Policy: Adapting Video Model for Control &amp; Planning ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>, we discussed that Cosmos Policy’s policy and world model training involves additional targets which provide auxiliary supervision: the policy learns to jointly predict <math id="A1.T4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(a,s^{\prime},v(s^{\prime}))|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(a,s^{\prime},v(s^{\prime}))|s)</annotation></semantics></math> instead of <math id="A1.T4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(a|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(a|s)</annotation></semantics></math>, and the world model learns to jointly predict <math id="A1.T4.m10" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p(s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> instead of <math id="A1.T4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(s^{\prime}|s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(s^{\prime}|s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>. To evaluate the effect of this joint learning objective, we train a version of Cosmos Policy without it by masking the loss on the additional targets: the policy predicts only <math id="A1.T4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(a|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(a|s)</annotation></semantics></math> and the world model predicts only <math id="A1.T4.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(s^{\prime}|s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(s^{\prime}|s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> (the value function continues to predict <math id="A1.T4.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(V(s^{\prime})|s,a,s^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(V(s^{\prime})|s,a,s^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> as before). We find that removing the auxiliary objectives leads to a 1.5 point drop in average success rate. (2) We also train a version of Cosmos Policy from scratch and observe a 3.9 point drop from the full version.
