<div id="A1.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To further study the effects of individual components of the Cosmos Policy design, as well as the joint training objectives discussed in Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Joint Training of Policy, World Model, &amp; Value Function ‣ 4 Cosmos Policy: Adapting Video Model for Control &amp; Planning ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>, we conduct a series of additional ablation experiments that remove individual components or objectives one at a time, until we ultimately have a barebones policy that only predicts actions (no future state or value). Recall from Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Joint Training of Policy, World Model, &amp; Value Function ‣ 4 Cosmos Policy: Adapting Video Model for Control &amp; Planning ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a> that Cosmos Policy is trained with a joint objective that optimizes the policy, world model, and value function altogether in one architecture. Specifically, each batch of training samples is split 50/25/25: 50 percent of the samples are used for training the policy, 25 percent for the world model, and 25 percent for the value function. This balanced splitting determines which parts of the latent diffusion are used as conditioning and which parts are used as the target, which in turn determines whether we are training the policy, the world model, or the value function (see Figure <a href="#A1.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ A.4.1 Additional Ablation Experiments ‣ A.4 Additional Experiments and Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> for an illustration). In addition to these balanced batches, the policy and world model are trained with auxiliary objectives: the policy learns to jointly predict <math id="A1.SS4.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(a,s^{\prime},v(s^{\prime}))|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(a,s^{\prime},v(s^{\prime}))|s)</annotation></semantics></math> instead of <math id="A1.SS4.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(a|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(a|s)</annotation></semantics></math>, and the world model learns to jointly predict <math id="A1.SS4.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p(s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> instead of <math id="A1.SS4.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(s^{\prime}|s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(s^{\prime}|s,a)</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F12" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.16163v1/fig/balanced_batches_figure.001.jpeg" id="A1.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:548/473;" width="548" height="473" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 12: </span><span id="A1.F12.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cosmos Policy balanced batches training scheme.</span> We illustrate the joint objectives training scheme discussed in Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Joint Training of Policy, World Model, &amp; Value Function ‣ 4 Cosmos Policy: Adapting Video Model for Control &amp; Planning ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>. While each batch of training samples is split 50/25/25 for policy, world model, and value function training, respectively, the full latent diffusion sequence remains fixed, and the conditioning scheme determines which of the three functions is being optimized. During training, the model is tasked to denoise the target noised latent frames conditioned on the clean latent frames. Note that the above depicts the initial base policy training scheme. When optionally refining the world model and value function on policy rollouts (in preparation for model-based planning), we mask out the current state and action during value function training so that the value predictions are only a function of the future state <math id="A1.F12.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>. Separately, to train a Q-value function, we can instead mask out the future state so that the value predictions are only a function of the current state and action, <math id="A1.F12.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>; this variant can be used for model-free planning (though we find that the model-based planning variant performs better, as shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 5.3 Evaluations of Cosmos Policy with Model-Based Planning ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>).
</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A1.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span><span id="A1.T5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cosmos Policy ablations and additional experiments in RoboCasa.</span> <span id="A1.T5.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top:</span> We ablate individual components of the joint objectives training scheme and auxiliary supervision discussed in Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Joint Training of Policy, World Model, &amp; Value Function ‣ 4 Cosmos Policy: Adapting Video Model for Control &amp; Planning ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a> and visualized in Figure <a href="#A1.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ A.4.1 Additional Ablation Experiments ‣ A.4 Additional Experiments and Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>. Each version of the policy is trained with the exact same training hyperparameters and compute as the original Cosmos Policy in RoboCasa, and evaluated across all 24 tasks with 50 trials per task and 3 random seeds (3600 trials total). We remove one component at a time until we arrive at a barebones policy that only predicts actions. Here are details describing each ablation: (1) We ablate value function training samples (last row of Figure <a href="#A1.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ A.4.1 Additional Ablation Experiments ‣ A.4 Additional Experiments and Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>) and instead use 50% of batches for policy training and 50% for world model training. (2) We ablate both world model and value function training samples (last two rows of Figure <a href="#A1.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ A.4.1 Additional Ablation Experiments ‣ A.4 Additional Experiments and Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>) and instead use 100% of each training batch for policy training only. (3) Adding to the prior ablation, we also ablate the value target when training the policy, thus optimizing the policy to learn just <math id="A1.T5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi(a,s^{\prime}|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi(a,s^{\prime}|s)</annotation></semantics></math> rather than <math id="A1.T5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi(a,s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi(a,s^{\prime},V(s^{\prime})|s)</annotation></semantics></math>. (4) Adding to the prior ablation, we ablate both the future state and value targets when training the policy, thus training a barebones policy that only models <math id="A1.T5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi(a|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi(a|s)</annotation></semantics></math>. We observe the most significant drop in performance from the final ablation, suggesting that training the policy to also predict future state is crucial to the effectiveness of Cosmos Policy. <span id="A1.T5.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bottom:</span> We also report the performance of Cosmos Policy with just 1 denoising step per action chunk at inference time. We observe a 66.4% average success rate with just 0.16 second inference latency per action chunk of 32 timesteps on one H100 GPU, which is nearly 4<math id="A1.T5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than the 0.61 second latency observed with 5 denoising steps with only a small hit (-0.5%) on success rate.
</figcaption>
<div id="A1.T5.8" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:397.5pt;height:50.1pt;vertical-align:-23.6pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-141.1pt,17.8pt) scale(0.584750557177582,0.584750557177582) ;">
<table id="A1.T5.8.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="A1.T5.8.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T5.8.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt"></th>
<th id="A1.T5.8.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt">Average SR (%)</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A1.T5.8.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T5.8.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">Cosmos Policy (ours) (5 denoising steps)</td>
<td id="A1.T5.8.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">67.1</td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T5.8.1.3" class="ltx_tr">

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.4.2 </span>Cosmos Policy Inference Latency</h4>

<div id="A1.SS4.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS4.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here we discuss measurements of inference latency in terms of wall-clock time. Cosmos Policy generates action, future state, and value predictions in parallel in 0.61 seconds total on 1 H100 GPU when sampling with 5 denoising steps (for LIBERO and RoboCasa). Inference latency increases to 0.95 seconds on 1 H100 GPU when sampling with 10 denoising steps (for ALOHA). Inference latency decreases to 0.16 seconds on 1 H100 GPU when sampling with 1 denoising step. We observe competitive performance in RoboCasa (66.4% average success rate) even with 1 denoising step, as shown in Table <a href="#A1.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ A.4.1 Additional Ablation Experiments ‣ A.4 Additional Experiments and Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. Note that these latencies are the time spent generating an action <em id="A1.SS4.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">chunk</em>. For example, on the ALOHA robot, the robot pauses for 0.95 seconds to generate an action chunk that spans 2 seconds of execution.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS4.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For model-based planning experiments on the real ALOHA robot, we do best-of-N search with <math id="A1.SS4.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=8</annotation></semantics></math> using 8 parallel H100 GPUs (1 for each branch in the search). Cosmos Policy first generates <math id="A1.SS4.SSS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> candidate action chunks with 10 denoising steps each, then generates an ensemble of 3 future state predictions per action proposal with 5 denoising steps each, and then generates an ensemble of 5 value predictions per future state prediction with 5 denoising steps each. In total, this search takes 4.9 seconds on 8 parallel H100 GPUs.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS4.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Though the high inference latency did not prevent effective task execution in our evaluations, we acknowledge the limitations caused by slow inference, such as difficulty in adapting the method to dynamic manipulation tasks or locomotion tasks. Optimizing the inference speed for the policy and the model-based search process would be a promising avenue for future work in order to enable adoption to a wide variety of robotics applications.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
</article>
